AML case management: from alert to SAR decision

MT

Mehak Tariq, CAMSNovember 25, 2026•8 min read

AML case management is the process, and the software behind it, that a bank or fintech uses to take unusual activity from the first alert or referral to a documented outcome: close it, keep watching, or file a suspicious activity report (SAR). A case groups the alerts, accounts, research and notes on one customer or relationship, tracks who owns each step, and keeps the record an examiner will test. The filing decision belongs to a named person or committee.

This guide explains public guidance and is not legal advice.

Where case management sits in the BSA program

The Bank Secrecy Act program rule for banks, 31 CFR 1020.210, requires risk-based customer due diligence that includes "ongoing monitoring to identify and report suspicious transactions". Case management is how a team carries out that duty.

The FFIEC BSA/AML Examination Manual splits suspicious activity monitoring into five components, and a case system carries the work after the first one, the alert. The manual expects a process to evaluate unusual activity "regardless of the method of identification", so route employee referrals and law enforcement inquiries into the same process as monitoring alerts.

The life of a case, from alert to SAR decision

This is one common way to run a case. Your procedure sets the tiers and internal deadlines.

StageWhat the system doesWhat the investigator decidesWhat is recorded
1. IntakeReceives the alert or referral, checks for open cases, assigns a queueWhether the item joins an existing caseSource, rule or referral type, time received
2. L1 reviewShows the CDD and EDD profile, the transactions and earlier alertsClose with a reason, or escalateData reviewed, rationale, reviewer, time
3. Case openedGroups related alerts and linked accounts into one caseWhich accounts and period to reviewCase scope and linked alerts
4. InvestigationTracks requests for information, searches and documentsWhether the activity is suspicious, and when that was determinedResearch steps, documents, determination date
5. RecommendationCollects the conclusion, the narrative draft and supporting documentsWhether to recommend filingConclusion and recommendation, with reasons
6. SAR decisionRoutes the case to the decision maker or committee and shows the deadlineFile or do not fileDecision, decision maker, specific reason
7. Filing and follow-upMarks supporting documentation, starts retention, schedules follow-upAccount actions and later reviewsFiling date, follow-up dates

The FFIEC manual says that after research, "investigators should document conclusions including any recommendation regarding whether or not to file a SAR." A law enforcement request opens a case without deciding it: "Mere receipt of any law enforcement inquiry does not, by itself, require the filing of a SAR". A SAR filed after a National Security Letter should not refer to it, and law enforcement discourages any reference to a grand jury subpoena in the SAR; keep both in the case file only.

The deadline runs from the determination in stage 4. Under 31 CFR 1020.320(b)(3), a bank files no later than 30 calendar days after initial detection of facts that may constitute a basis for filing. It gets up to 30 more days if no suspect has been identified on the date of detection, and no more than 60 in total. The FFIEC explains that the period starts when the bank "knows or has reason to suspect that the activity or transactions under review meet one or more of the definitions of suspicious activity". Make the determination date, and who made it, required fields.

What an AML case file must contain for examiners

When examiners test suspicious activity reporting, the FFIEC examination procedures say the examiner "should follow an alert through the entire process." They sample research decisions to check whether decisions to file or not file "are supported and reasonable", whether "documentation is adequate", and whether "the decision process is completed and SARs are filed in a timely manner". A case file that answers them without the investigator in the room holds:

  • the source: alert IDs and rules, or the referral or law enforcement request that opened the case;
  • the customer's CDD and EDD information as it stood at review, since examiners check whether the SAR decision process "appropriately considers all available CDD and EDD information";
  • the accounts, period and transactions reviewed, and each research step and its result;
  • the investigator's conclusion and recommendation, and the date the activity was determined suspicious;
  • the decision, who made it and the specific reason;
  • for a filed SAR: a copy, the filing date and the supporting documentation, marked as such;
  • follow-up: continuing activity reviews, account decisions and board reporting.

Supporting documentation has a legal meaning. 31 CFR 1020.320(d) requires a bank to keep a copy of each SAR and its supporting documentation for five years from the date of filing, and says supporting documentation "shall be identified, and maintained by the bank as such, and shall be deemed to have been filed with the SAR." The FFIEC defines it as "all documents or records that assisted a bank in making the determination that certain activity required a SAR filing." The case system needs a way to flag those documents and produce them on request.

Decisions not to file need a rule in your procedure. The manual's text says to document the reason for filing or not filing, but it now points examiners to the October 2025 interagency SAR FAQs as the most current guidance. Those FAQs say there is "no requirement or expectation" to document a decision not to file, and that any documentation "need not exceed that which is necessary for the institution's internal policies, procedures, and controls". Examiners still sample decisions not to file, so set what a closed case records, even if it is one line.

Escalation from L1 to L2 to the SAR committee

Tier names are a team convention; the regulations do not use them. At any size, the manual expects a defined escalation path from first detection to the end of the investigation. A three-tier model:

  • L1 analysts close alerts with a reason or escalate them.
  • L2 investigators work the case, determine whether the activity is suspicious and write the recommendation.
  • A SAR decision maker or committee holds the authority for the final filing decision. For a committee, the manual says "there should be a clearly defined process to resolve differences of opinion on filing decisions."

Under the FFIEC's internal controls section, employees who complete reporting forms such as SARs "generally should not also be responsible for the decision to file the reports", so the system should stop one user from preparing and deciding the same case, with a documented exception path for small teams. The SAR section adds that the board, or a board committee, must be told that SARs have been filed.

Some cases need their own path. For violations that require immediate attention, such as ongoing money laundering schemes, 31 CFR 1020.320(b)(3) requires the bank to "immediately notify, by telephone, an appropriate law enforcement authority in addition to filing timely a SAR." For repeat SAR filings on an account, the manual says escalation procedures should include review by senior management and legal staff, and criteria for whether to close the account and when to notify law enforcement.

A separate continuing activity review is a choice. The SAR FAQs say a bank "is not required to conduct a separate review" after a filing, and may instead rely on risk-based policies reasonably designed to identify and report continuing activity. For banks that follow FinCEN's continuing activity guidance, the FAQs give a timeline for a SAR with an identified subject: detection on day 0, the first SAR by day 30, the end of the 90-day period on day 120 and the next SAR by day 150.

Quality assurance and the metrics a team tracks

The FFIEC says independent testing may include evaluating filed or prepared SARs "to determine their accuracy, timeliness, completeness, and conformance to the bank's policies, procedures, and processes." Inside the team, a reviewer who did not work the case can re-check a sample of closed alerts, no-file decisions and filed SARs against the case file list above. Metrics to track:

  • open alerts and cases by age, against your internal targets;
  • cases approaching the filing deadline, counted from the determination date;
  • the L1 escalation rate, and L1 closures that QA or L2 reversed;
  • QA findings by type, such as missing documents or unsupported rationale;
  • SARs filed in the period, for board reporting.

Put staffing in the same report: the examination procedures say "The volume of system alerts and investigations should not be tailored solely to meet existing staffing levels."

What AML case management software must support

The banking agencies and FinCEN do not favor a particular method or technology. In their 2018 joint statement on innovative efforts, the Federal Reserve, FDIC, FinCEN, NCUA and OCC said they "will not advocate a particular method or technology for banks to comply with BSA/AML requirements." Whether you buy an AML case management system or configure a general workflow tool, check that it can:

  • take alerts and referrals from every source, including monitoring, sanctions screening, employee referrals and law enforcement requests, into one queue;
  • group alerts into cases by customer and relationship, with CDD, EDD and account data in the case;
  • enforce your workflow: tiers, required fields before closure, and a decision-maker role the preparer cannot also hold, unless a documented exception applies;
  • track deadlines from the determination date, including the 30- and 60-day limits and any continuing activity dates;
  • keep a history of every change, showing who did what and when, that users cannot edit;
  • flag supporting documentation and keep it for at least five years from filing;
  • restrict access, because under 31 CFR 1020.320(e) a SAR and "any information that would reveal the existence of a SAR, are confidential";
  • report the metrics above, and offer an API so other systems can add data and notes.

Common questions

What are the steps of AML case management?

No regulation sets a number. The FFIEC's five monitoring components are the closest official outline, and a team can turn them into stages like the seven in the table above.

What are the 5 pillars of AML?

For banks the phrase matches the five minimum elements in 31 CFR 1020.210: internal controls, independent testing, a designated individual responsible for day-to-day compliance, training, and risk-based customer due diligence.

What is the best AML software for banks?

The agencies do not name one. The right choice depends on your alert sources, volumes, team structure and record rules, so test a shortlist of AML case management tools against the checklist above on your own past cases.

Do we have to document a decision not to file a SAR?

Under the October 2025 interagency FAQs, no. If you choose to, a short statement will usually do.
